{{Short description|Statistical method}}
{{Other uses|Bootstrapping (disambiguation)}}

'''Bootstrapping''' is a procedure for estimating the distribution of an [[Estimator|estimator]] by [[Resampling (statistics)|resampling]] (often with [[Sampling (statistics)#Replacement of selected units|replacement]]) one's data or a model which is estimated from the data.<ref name=Horowitz2019/> Bootstrapping assigns measures of accuracy ([[Bias (statistics)|bias]], variance, [[confidence interval]]s, prediction error, etc.) to sample estimates.<ref name="et1993">{{cite book |last1=Efron |first1= B. |author-link1=Bradley Efron |last2= Tibshirani |first2= R. |author-link2=Robert Tibshirani |name-list-style=vanc|title = An Introduction to the Bootstrap |publisher = Chapman & Hall/CRC |location=Boca Raton, FL |year = 1993 |isbn = 0-412-04231-2}} [http://lib.stat.cmu.edu/S/bootstrap.funs software] {{Webarchive|url=https://archive.today/20120712124533/http://lib.stat.cmu.edu/S/bootstrap.funs |date=2012-07-12 }}</ref><ref>
{{cite journal |last1=Efron |first1=Bradley|name-list-style=vanc|title=Second thoughts on the bootstrap|journal=Statistical Science |date=2003|volume=18|number=2|pages=135–140|doi=10.1214/ss/1063994968 |bibcode=2003StaSc..1894968E |url=https://projecteuclid.org/journals/statistical-science/volume-18/issue-2/Second-Thoughts-on-the-Bootstrap/10.1214/ss/1063994968.pdf}}</ref> This technique allows estimation of the sampling distribution of almost any statistic using random sampling methods.<ref name="Horowitz2019">{{cite journal |last1=Horowitz |first1=Joel L. |name-list-style=vanc|title=Bootstrap methods in econometrics |journal=Annual Review of Economics |date=2019 |volume=11 |pages=193–224 |doi=10.1146/annurev-economics-080218-025651|doi-access=free|arxiv=1809.04016 }}</ref>

Bootstrapping estimates the properties of an [[estimand]] (such as its [[variance]]) by measuring those properties when sampling from an approximating distribution. One standard choice for an approximating distribution is the [[empirical distribution function]] of the observed data. In the case where a set of observations can be assumed to be from an [[independent and identically distributed]] population, this can be implemented by constructing a number of  [[Resampling (statistics)|resamples]] with replacement, of the observed data set (and of equal size to the observed data set). A key result in Efron's seminal paper that introduced the bootstrap<ref name="Efron1979"/> is the favorable performance of bootstrap methods using [[Sampling (statistics)#Replacement of selected units|sampling with replacement]] compared to prior methods like the [[jackknife resampling|jackknife]] that sample without replacement. However, since its introduction, numerous variants on the bootstrap have been proposed, including methods that sample without replacement or that create bootstrap samples larger or smaller than the original data.

The bootstrap may also be used for constructing [[statistical hypothesis testing|hypothesis tests]].<ref>Lehmann E.L. (1992) "Introduction to Neyman and Pearson (1933) On the Problem of the Most Efficient Tests of Statistical Hypotheses". In: Breakthroughs in Statistics, Volume 1, (Eds Kotz, S., Johnson, N.L.), Springer-Verlag. ISBN 0-387-94037-5 (followed by reprinting of the paper).</ref> It is often used as an alternative to [[statistical inference]] based on the assumption of a parametric model when that assumption is in doubt, or where parametric inference is impossible or requires complicated formulas for the calculation of [[standard error]]s.

== Approach ==
[[File: Illustration bootstrap.svg|thumb|400px|A sample is drawn from a population. From this sample, resamples are generated by drawing with replacement (orange). Data points that were drawn more than once (which happens for approx. 26.4% of data points) are shown in red and slightly offsetted. From the resamples, the statistic <math>x</math> is calculated and, therefore, a histogram can be calculated to estimate the distribution of <math>x</math>.]]
The basic idea of bootstrapping is that inference about a population from sample data (sample → population) can be modeled by ''resampling'' the sample data and performing inference about a sample from resampled data (resampled → sample).<ref>Good, P. (2006) Resampling Methods. 3rd Ed. Birkhauser.</ref> As the population is unknown, the true error in a sample statistic against its population value is unknown. In bootstrap-resamples, the 'population' is in fact the sample, and this is known; hence the quality of inference of the 'true' sample from resampled data (resampled → sample) is measurable.

More formally, the bootstrap works by treating inference of the true [[probability distribution]] ''J'', given the original data, as being analogous to an inference of the empirical distribution ''Ĵ'', given the resampled data. The accuracy of inferences regarding ''Ĵ'' using the resampled data can be assessed because we know ''Ĵ''. If ''Ĵ'' is a reasonable approximation to ''J'', then the quality of inference on ''J'' can in turn be inferred.

As an example, assume we are interested in the average (or [[mean]]) height of people worldwide.  We cannot measure all the people in the global population, so instead, we sample only a tiny part of it, and measure that.  Assume the sample is of size ''N''; that is, we measure the heights of ''N'' individuals.  From that single sample, only one estimate of the mean can be obtained.  In order to reason about the population, we need some sense of the [[Statistical dispersion|variability]] of the mean that we have computed. The simplest bootstrap method involves taking the original data set of heights, and, using a computer, sampling from it to form a new sample (called a 'resample' or bootstrap sample) that is also of size&nbsp;''N''.  The bootstrap sample is taken from the original by using [[Simple random sample|sampling with replacement]] (e.g. we might 'resample' 5 times from [1,2,3,4,5] and get [2,5,4,4,1]), so, assuming ''N'' is sufficiently large, for all practical purposes there is virtually zero probability that it will be identical to the original "real" sample.  This process is repeated a large number of times (typically 1,000 or 10,000 times), and for each of these bootstrap samples, we compute its mean (each of these is called a "bootstrap estimate").  We now can create a histogram of bootstrap means.  This histogram provides an estimate of the shape of the distribution of the sample mean from which we can answer questions about how much the mean varies across samples.  (The method here, described for the mean, can be applied to almost any other [[statistic]] or [[estimator]].)

== Discussion ==

{{no footnotes|section|date=June 2012}}

=== Advantages ===
A great advantage of bootstrap is its simplicity. It is a straightforward way to derive estimates of [[standard error (statistics)|standard errors]] and [[confidence intervals]] for complex estimators of the distribution, such as percentile points, proportions, [[Odds ratio]], and correlation coefficients. However, despite its simplicity, bootstrapping can be applied to complex sampling designs (e.g. for population divided into s strata with n<sub>s</sub> observations per strata, one example of which is a dose-response experiment, where bootstrapping can be applied for each stratum).<ref name="ch21_brm" /> Bootstrap is also an appropriate way to control and check the stability of the results.  Although for most problems it is impossible to know the true confidence interval, bootstrap is asymptotically more accurate than the standard intervals obtained using sample variance and assumptions of normality.<ref name=DiCiccio1996>{{cite journal
| last1 = DiCiccio | first1 = Thomas J. | last2 = Efron | first2 = Bradley | author2-link = Bradley Efron | name-list-style=vanc | year = 1996 | title = Bootstrap confidence intervals (with Discussion) | journal = Statistical Science | volume = 11 | pages = 189–228 | number = 3 | doi = 10.1214/ss/1032280214 | doi-access = free}}</ref> Bootstrapping is also a convenient method that avoids the cost of repeating the experiment to get other groups of sample data.

=== Disadvantages ===
Bootstrapping depends heavily on the estimator used and, though simple, naive use of bootstrapping will not always yield asymptotically valid results and can lead to inconsistency.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Hinkley|first=David|name-list-style=vanc|year=1994|title=[Bootstrap: More than a Stab in the Dark?]: Comment|journal=Statistical Science|volume=9|number=3|pages=400–403|doi=10.1214/ss/1177010387|issn=0883-4237|doi-access=free}}</ref> Although bootstrapping is (under some conditions) asymptotically [[Consistency (statistics)|consistent]], it does not provide general finite-sample guarantees. The result may depend on the representative sample. The apparent simplicity may conceal the fact that important assumptions are being made when undertaking the bootstrap analysis (e.g. independence of samples or large enough of a sample size) where these would be more formally stated in other approaches. Also, bootstrapping can be time-consuming and there are not many available software for bootstrapping as it is difficult to automate using traditional statistical computer packages.<ref name="ch21_brm" />

=== Recommendations ===

Scholars have recommended more bootstrap samples as available computing power has increased. If the results may have substantial real-world consequences, then one should use as many samples as is reasonable, given available computing power and time. Increasing the number of samples cannot increase the amount of information in the original data; it can only reduce the effects of random sampling errors which can arise from a bootstrap procedure itself. Moreover, there is evidence that numbers of samples greater than 100 lead to negligible improvements in the estimation of standard errors.<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Goodhue | first1=Dale L.|last2=Lewis|first2=William|last3=Thompson|first3=William|name-list-style=vanc | year=2012 | title=Does PLS have advantages for small sample size or non-normal data? | journal=[[MIS Quarterly]] | volume=36 | number=3 | pages=981–1001 | doi=10.2307/41703490 | jstor=41703490 | id = [https://www.misq.org/skin/frontend/default/misq/pdf/appendices/2012/V36I3_Appendices/GoodhueResearchNoteAppendix.pdf Appendix]}}</ref> In fact, according to the original developer of the bootstrapping method, even setting the number of samples at 50 is likely to lead to fairly good standard error estimates.<ref>Efron, B., Rogosa, D., & Tibshirani, R. (2004). Resampling methods of estimation. In N.J. Smelser, & P.B. Baltes (Eds.). International Encyclopedia of the Social & Behavioral Sciences (pp. 13216–13220). New York, NY: Elsevier.</ref>

Adèr et al. recommend the bootstrap procedure for the following situations:<ref name=Ader/>

:*When the theoretical distribution of a statistic of interest is complicated or unknown. Since the bootstrapping procedure is distribution-independent it provides an indirect method to assess the properties of the distribution underlying the sample and the parameters of interest that are derived from this distribution.

:*When the [[sample size]] is insufficient for straightforward statistical inference. If the underlying distribution is well-known, bootstrapping provides a way to account for the distortions caused by the specific sample that may not be fully representative of the population.

:* When [[statistical power|power calculations]] have to be performed, and a small pilot sample is available. Most power and sample size calculations are heavily dependent on the standard deviation of the statistic of interest. If the estimate used is incorrect, the required sample size will also be wrong. One method to get an impression of the variation of the statistic is to use a small pilot sample and perform bootstrapping on it to get impression of the variance.

However, Athreya has shown<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Athreya | first1 = K. B. | name-list-style = vanc | year = 1987 | title = Bootstrap of the mean in the infinite variance case | journal = [[Annals of Statistics]] | volume=15 | number=2 | pages = 724–731|doi=10.1214/aos/1176350371|doi-access=free}}</ref> that if one performs a naive bootstrap on the sample mean when the underlying population lacks a finite variance (for example, a [[power law distribution]]), then the bootstrap distribution will not converge to the same limit as the sample mean. As a result, confidence intervals on the basis of a [[Monte Carlo simulation]] of the bootstrap could be misleading. Athreya states that "Unless one is reasonably sure that the underlying distribution is not [[Heavy-tailed distribution|heavy tailed]], one should hesitate to use the naive bootstrap".

== Types of bootstrap scheme ==
{{no footnotes|section|date=June 2012}}

In univariate problems, it is usually acceptable to resample the individual observations with replacement ("case resampling" below) unlike [[Resampling (statistics)#Subsampling|subsampling]], in which resampling is without replacement and is valid under much weaker conditions compared to the bootstrap. In small samples, a parametric bootstrap approach might be preferred. For other problems, a ''smooth bootstrap'' will likely be preferred.

For regression problems, various other alternatives are available.<ref name="et1993" />

=== Case resampling ===
The bootstrap is generally useful for estimating the distribution of a statistic (e.g. mean, variance) without using normality assumptions (as required, e.g., for a z-statistic or a t-statistic). In particular, the bootstrap is useful when there is no analytical form or an asymptotic theory (e.g., an applicable [[central limit theorem]]) to help estimate the distribution of the statistics of interest. This is because bootstrap methods can apply to most random quantities, e.g., the ratio of variance and mean. There are at least two ways of performing case resampling.

# The Monte Carlo algorithm for case resampling is quite simple. First, we resample the data with replacement, and the size of the resample must be equal to the size of the original data set. Then the statistic of interest is computed from the resample from the first step. We repeat this routine many times to get a more precise estimate of the Bootstrap distribution of the statistic.<ref name="et1993" />
# The 'exact' version for case resampling is similar, but we exhaustively enumerate every possible resample of the data set. This can be computationally expensive as there are a total of <math>\binom {2n-1}n = \frac{(2n-1)!}{n! (n-1)!}</math> different resamples, where ''n'' is the size of the data set. Thus for ''n''&nbsp;=&nbsp;5,&nbsp;10,&nbsp;20,&nbsp;30 there are 126, 92378, 6.89&nbsp;×&nbsp;10<sup>10</sup> and 5.91&nbsp;×&nbsp;10<sup>16</sup>  different resamples respectively.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://statweb.stanford.edu/~susan/courses/s208/node37.html |title=How many different bootstrap samples are there? Statweb.stanford.edu |access-date=2019-12-09 |archive-date=2019-09-14 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190914102512/http://statweb.stanford.edu/~susan/courses/s208/node37.html |url-status=dead }}</ref>

==== Estimating the distribution of sample mean ====
Consider a coin-flipping experiment. We flip the coin and record whether it lands heads or tails. Let {{nowrap|''X {{=}} x''<sub>1</sub>, ''x''<sub>2</sub>, …, ''x''<sub>10</sub>}} be 10 observations from the experiment. {{nowrap|''x<sub>i</sub>'' {{=}} 1}} if the flip lands heads, and 0 otherwise. By invoking the assumption that the average of the coin flips is normally distributed, we can use the [[Student's t-statistic|t-statistic]] to estimate the distribution of the sample mean,

: <math> \bar{x} = \frac{1}{10} (x_1 + x_2 + \cdots + x_{10}).</math>

Such a normality assumption can be justified either as an approximation of the distribution of each ''individual'' coin flip or as an approximation of the distribution of the ''average'' of a large number of coin flips. The former is a poor approximation because the true distribution of the coin flips is [[Bernoulli distribution|Bernoulli]] instead of normal. The latter is a valid approximation in ''infinitely large'' samples due to the [[central limit theorem]].

However, if we are not ready to make such a justification, then we can use the bootstrap instead. Using case resampling, we can derive the distribution of <math> \bar{x}</math>. We first resample the data to obtain a ''bootstrap resample''. An example of the first resample might look like this {{nowrap|''X''<sub>1</sub>* {{=}} ''x''<sub>2</sub>, ''x''<sub>1</sub>, ''x''<sub>10</sub>, ''x''<sub>10</sub>, ''x''<sub>3</sub>, ''x''<sub>4</sub>, ''x''<sub>6</sub>, ''x''<sub>7</sub>, ''x''<sub>1</sub>, ''x''<sub>9</sub>}}. There are some duplicates since a bootstrap resample comes from sampling with replacement from the data. Also the number of data points in a bootstrap resample is equal to the number of data points in our original observations. Then we compute the mean of this resample and obtain the first ''bootstrap mean'': ''μ''<sub>1</sub>*. We repeat this process to obtain the second resample ''X''<sub>2</sub>* and compute the second bootstrap mean ''μ''<sub>2</sub>*. If we repeat this 100 times, then we have ''μ''<sub>1</sub>*, ''μ''<sub>2</sub>*, ..., ''μ''<sub>100</sub>*.  This represents an ''empirical bootstrap distribution'' of sample mean. From this empirical distribution, one can derive a ''bootstrap confidence interval'' for the purpose of hypothesis testing.

==== Regression ====

In regression problems, ''case resampling'' refers to the simple scheme of resampling individual cases – often rows of a [[data set]]. For regression problems, as long as the data set is fairly large, this simple scheme is often acceptable.{{Citation needed|date=August 2024}} However, the method is open to criticism{{Citation needed|date=April 2009}}.<ref name="ch21_brm">{{Cite web|title=21 Bootstrapping Regression Models|url=https://www.sagepub.com/sites/default/files/upm-binaries/21122_Chapter_21.pdf|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150724033201/http://www.sagepub.com:80/sites/default/files/upm-binaries/21122_Chapter_21.pdf |archive-date=2015-07-24 }}</ref>

In regression problems, the [[explanatory variable]]s are often fixed, or at least observed with more control than the response variable. Also, the range of the explanatory variables defines the information available from them. Therefore, to resample cases means that each bootstrap sample will lose some information. As such, alternative bootstrap procedures should be considered.

=== Bayesian bootstrap ===
Bootstrapping can be interpreted in a [[Bayesian probability|Bayesian]] framework using a scheme that creates new data sets through reweighting the initial data. Given a set of <math>N</math> data points, the weighting assigned to data point <math>i</math> in a new data set <math>\mathcal{D}^J</math> is <math>w^J_i = x^J_i - x^J_{i-1}</math>, where <math>\mathbf{x}^J</math> is a low-to-high ordered list of <math>N-1</math> uniformly distributed random numbers on <math>[0,1]</math>, preceded by 0 and succeeded by 1. The distributions of a parameter inferred from considering many such data sets <math>\mathcal{D}^J</math> are then interpretable as [[posterior distribution]]s on that parameter.<ref>Rubin, D. B. (1981). "The Bayesian bootstrap". ''[[Annals of Statistics]]'', 9, 130.</ref>

=== Smooth bootstrap ===
Under this scheme, a small amount of (usually normally distributed) zero-centered random noise is added onto each resampled observation. This is equivalent to sampling from a [[kernel density]] estimate of the data. Assume ''K'' to be a symmetric kernel density function with unit variance. The standard kernel estimator <math>\hat{f\,}_h(x)</math> of <math>f(x)</math> is

: <math>\hat{f\,}_h(x)={1\over nh}\sum_{i=1}^nK\left({x-X_i\over h}\right),</math>&nbsp;<ref name="wang1995">{{Cite journal|last=WANG|first=SUOJIN|title=Optimizing the smoothed bootstrap|date=1995|journal=Ann. Inst. Statist. Math.|volume=47|pages=65–80|doi=10.1007/BF00773412|s2cid=122041565}}</ref>

where <math>h</math> is the smoothing parameter. And the corresponding distribution function estimator <math>\hat{F\,}_h(x)</math> is

: <math>\hat{F\,}_h(x)=\int_{-\infty}^x \hat f_h(t)\,dt.</math>&nbsp;<ref name="wang1995"/>

=== Parametric bootstrap ===
Based on the assumption that the original data set is a realization of a random sample from a distribution of a specific parametric type, in this case a parametric model is fitted by parameter θ,  often by [[maximum likelihood]], and samples of [[random number generation|random numbers]] are drawn from this fitted model. Usually the sample drawn has the same sample size as the original data. Then the estimate of original function F can be written as <math>\hat{F}=F_{\hat{\theta}}</math>. This sampling process is repeated many times as for other bootstrap methods. Considering the centered [[Sample means|sample mean]] in this case, the random sample original distribution function <math>F_{\theta}</math> is replaced by a bootstrap random sample with function <math>F_{\hat{\theta}}</math>, and the [[probability distribution]] of <math>\bar{X_{n}}-\mu_{\theta}</math> is approximated by that of <math>\bar{X}_n^*-\mu^*</math>, where <math>\mu^*=\mu_{\hat{\theta}}</math>, which is the expectation corresponding to <math>F_{\hat{\theta}}</math>.<ref>{{Cite book|title=A modern introduction to probability and statistics : understanding why and how|date=2005|publisher=Springer|last1=Dekking|first1=Frederik Michel|last2=Kraaikamp|first2=Cornelis|last3=Lopuhaä|first3=Hendrik Paul|last4=Meester|first4=Ludolf Erwin|isbn=978-1-85233-896-1|location=London|oclc=262680588}}</ref> The use of a parametric model at the sampling stage of the bootstrap methodology leads to procedures which are different from those obtained by applying basic statistical theory to inference for the same model{{Citation needed|reason=No reasoning or context is given for this claim.|date=February 2026}}.

=== Resampling residuals ===
Another approach to bootstrapping in regression problems is to resample [[Errors and residuals in statistics|residual]]s. The method proceeds as follows.

# Fit the model and retain the fitted values <math>\widehat{y\,}_i</math> and the residuals <math>\widehat{\varepsilon\,}_i = y_i - \widehat{y\,}_i, (i = 1,\dots, n)</math>.
# For each pair, (''x<sub>i</sub>'', ''y<sub>i</sub>''), in which ''x<sub>i</sub>'' is the (possibly multivariate) explanatory variable, add a randomly resampled residual, <math>\widehat{\varepsilon\,}_j</math>, to the fitted value <math>\widehat{y\,}_i</math>. In other words, create synthetic response variables <math>y^*_i = \widehat{y\,}_i + \widehat{\varepsilon\,}_j</math> where ''j'' is selected randomly from the list (1, ..., ''n'') for every ''i''.
# Refit the model using the fictitious response variables <math>y^*_i</math>, and retain the quantities of interest (often the parameters, <math>\widehat\mu^*_i</math>, estimated from the synthetic <math>y^*_i</math>).
# Repeat steps 2 and 3 a large number of times.

This scheme has the advantage that it retains the information in the explanatory variables. However, a question arises as to which residuals to resample. Raw residuals are one option; another is [[studentized residuals]] (in linear regression). Although there are arguments in favor of using studentized residuals; in practice, it often makes little difference, and it is easy to compare the results of both schemes.

=== Gaussian process regression bootstrap ===
When data are temporally correlated, straightforward bootstrapping destroys the inherent correlations. This method uses Gaussian process regression (GPR) to fit a probabilistic model from which replicates may then be drawn. GPR is a Bayesian non-linear regression method. A Gaussian process (GP) is a collection of random variables, any finite number of which have a joint Gaussian (normal) distribution. A GP is defined by a mean function and a covariance function, which specify the mean vectors and covariance matrices for each finite collection of the random variables.<ref name="kirk2009">{{Cite journal|last=Kirk|first=Paul|date=2009|title=Gaussian process regression bootstrapping: exploring the effects of uncertainty in time course data|url= |journal=Bioinformatics|volume=25|issue=10|pages=1300–1306|doi=10.1093/bioinformatics/btp139|pmid=19289448|pmc=2677737}}</ref>

'''Regression model:'''

: <math>y(x)=f(x)+\varepsilon,\ \    \varepsilon\sim \mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2),</math> <math>\varepsilon</math> is a noise term.

'''Gaussian process prior:'''

For any finite collection of variables, ''x''<sub>1</sub>,&nbsp;...,&nbsp;''x''<sub>''n''</sub>, the function outputs <math>f(x_1),\ldots,f(x_n)</math> are jointly distributed according to a multivariate Gaussian with mean <math>m=[m(x_1),\ldots,m(x_n)]^\intercal
</math> and covariance matrix <math>(K)_{ij}=k(x_i,x_j).</math>

Assume <math>f(x)\sim \mathcal{GP}(m,k).</math> Then <math>y(x)\sim \mathcal{GP}(m,l)</math>,

where <math>l(x_i,x_j)=k(x_i,x_j)+\sigma^2\delta(x_i,x_j)</math>, and <math>\delta(x_i,x_j)</math> is the standard Kronecker delta function.<ref name="kirk2009" />

'''Gaussian process posterior:'''

According to GP prior, we can get

: <math>[y(x_1),\ldots,y(x_r)]\sim \mathcal{N}(m_0,K_0)
</math>,

where <math>m_0=[m(x_1),\ldots,m(x_r)]^\intercal</math> and <math>(K_0)_{ij}=k(x_i,x_j)+\sigma^2\delta(x_i,x_j).</math>

Let x<sub>1</sub><sup>*</sup>,...,x<sub>s</sub><sup>*</sup> be another finite collection of variables, it's obvious that

: <math>[y(x_1),\ldots,y(x_r),f(x_1^*),\ldots,f(x_s^*)]^\intercal\sim \mathcal{N}(\binom{m_0}{m_*}\begin{pmatrix} K_0 & K_* \\ K_*^\intercal & K_{**} \end{pmatrix})
</math>,

where <math>m_*=[m(x_1^*),\ldots,m(x_s^*)]^\intercal</math>, <math>(K_{**})_{ij}=k(x_i^*,x_j^*)</math>, <math>(K_*)_{ij}=k(x_i,x_j^*). </math>

According to the equations above, the outputs ''y'' are also jointly distributed according to a multivariate Gaussian. Thus,

: <math>[f(x_1^*),\ldots,f(x_s^*)]^\intercal\mid([y(x)]^\intercal=y)\sim \mathcal{N}(m_\text{post},K_\text{post}),</math>

where <math>y=[y_1,...,y_r]^\intercal</math>, <math>m_\text{post}=m_*+K_*^\intercal(K_O+\sigma^2I_r)^{-1}(y-m_0)</math>, <math>K_\text{post}=K_{**}-K_*^\intercal(K_O+\sigma^2I_r)^{-1}K_*</math>, and <math>I_r</math> is <math>r\times r</math> identity matrix.<ref name="kirk2009" />

=== Wild bootstrap ===
The wild bootstrap, proposed originally by Wu (1986),<ref>{{cite journal | title=Jackknife, bootstrap and other resampling methods in regression analysis (with discussions) | author=Wu, C.F.J. | journal=Annals of Statistics | year=1986 | volume=14 | pages=1261–1350 | doi=10.1214/aos/1176350142| doi-access=free }}</ref> is suited when the model exhibits [[heteroskedasticity]]. The idea is, as the residual bootstrap, to leave the regressors at their sample value, but to resample the response variable based on the residuals values. That is, for each replicate, one computes a new <math>y</math> based on

:<math>y^*_i = \widehat{y\,}_i + \widehat{\varepsilon\,}_i v_i</math>

so the residuals are randomly multiplied by a random variable <math>v_i</math> with mean 0 and variance 1. For most distributions of <math> v_i </math> (but not Mammen's), this method assumes that the 'true' residual distribution is symmetric and can offer advantages over simple residual sampling for smaller sample sizes. Different forms are used for the random variable <math>v_i</math>, such as

:*The [[standard normal distribution]]

:*A distribution suggested by Mammen (1993).<ref>{{cite journal | title=Bootstrap and wild bootstrap for high dimensional linear models | author=Mammen, E. | journal=Annals of Statistics |date=Mar 1993 | volume=21 | issue=1 | pages=255–285 | doi=10.1214/aos/1176349025| doi-access=free }}</ref>

:::<math> v_i = \begin{cases}
-(\sqrt{5} -1)/2 & \text{with probability } (\sqrt{5} +1)/(2\sqrt{5}), \\
(\sqrt{5} +1)/2 & \text{with probability } (\sqrt{5} -1)/(2\sqrt{5})
\end{cases}</math>

::Approximately, Mammen's distribution is:

:::<math> v_i = \begin{cases}
-0.6180\quad\text{(with a 0 in the units' place)} & \text{with probability } 0.7236, \\
+1.6180\quad\text{(with a 1 in the units' place)} & \text{with probability } 0.2764.
\end{cases}</math>

:*Or the simpler distribution, linked to the [[Rademacher distribution]]:

:::<math> v_i =\begin{cases}
-1 & \text{with probability } 1/2, \\
+1 & \text{with probability } 1/2.
\end{cases}</math>

=== Block bootstrap ===

The block bootstrap is used when the data, or the errors in a model, are correlated. In this case, a simple case or residual resampling will fail, as it is not able to replicate the correlation in the data. The block bootstrap tries to replicate the correlation by resampling inside blocks of data (see [[Blocking (statistics)]]). The block bootstrap has been used mainly with data correlated in time (i.e. time series) but can also be used with data correlated in space, or among groups (so-called cluster data).

==== Time series: Simple block bootstrap ====
In the (simple) block bootstrap, the variable of interest is split into non-overlapping blocks.

==== Time series: Moving block bootstrap ====

In the moving block bootstrap, introduced by Künsch (1989),<ref>{{cite journal |last=Künsch |first=H. R. |year=1989 |title=The Jackknife and the Bootstrap for General Stationary Observations |journal=Annals of Statistics |volume=17 |issue=3 |pages=1217–1241 |doi=10.1214/aos/1176347265 |doi-access=free }}</ref> data is split into ''n''&nbsp;−&nbsp;''b''&nbsp;+&nbsp;1 overlapping blocks of length ''b'': Observation 1 to b will be block 1, observation 2 to ''b''&nbsp;+&nbsp;1 will be block 2, etc. Then from these ''n''&nbsp;−&nbsp;''b''&nbsp;+&nbsp;1 blocks, ''n''/''b'' blocks will be drawn at random with replacement. Then aligning these n/b blocks in the order they were picked, will give the bootstrap observations.

This bootstrap works with dependent data, however, the bootstrapped observations will not be stationary anymore by construction. But, it was shown that varying randomly the block length can avoid this problem.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Politis |first1=D. N. |last2=Romano |first2=J. P. |year=1994 |title=The Stationary Bootstrap |journal=Journal of the American Statistical Association |volume=89 |issue=428 |pages=1303–1313 |doi=10.1080/01621459.1994.10476870 |bibcode=1994JASA...89.1303P |hdl=10983/25607 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> This method is known as the ''stationary bootstrap.'' Other related modifications of the moving block bootstrap are the ''Markovian bootstrap'' and a stationary bootstrap method that matches subsequent blocks based on standard deviation matching.

==== Time series: Maximum entropy bootstrap ====

Vinod (2006),<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Vinod|first=HD|date=2006|title=Maximum entropy ensembles for time series inference in economics|journal=Journal of Asian Economics|volume=17|issue=6|pages=955–978|doi=10.1016/j.asieco.2006.09.001}}</ref> presents a method that bootstraps time series data using  maximum entropy principles satisfying the Ergodic theorem with mean-preserving and mass-preserving constraints. There is an R package, '''meboot''',<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Vinod|first1=Hrishikesh|last2=López-de-Lacalle|first2=Javier|date=2009|title=Maximum entropy bootstrap for time series: The meboot R package|journal=Journal of Statistical Software|volume=29|issue=5|pages=1–19|doi=10.18637/jss.v029.i05 |doi-access=free}}</ref> that utilizes the method, which  has applications in econometrics and computer science.

==== Cluster data: block bootstrap ====
Cluster data describes data where many observations per unit are observed. This could be observing many firms in many states or observing students in many classes. In such cases, the correlation structure is simplified, and one does usually make the assumption that data is correlated within a group/cluster, but independent between groups/clusters. The structure of the block bootstrap is easily obtained (where the block just corresponds to the group), and usually only the groups are resampled, while the observations within the groups are left unchanged. [[A. Colin Cameron|Cameron]] et al. (2008) discusses this for clustered errors in linear regression.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Cameron |first1=A. C. |first2=J. B. |last2=Gelbach |first3=D. L. |last3=Miller |year=2008 |title=Bootstrap-based improvements for inference with clustered errors |journal=[[Review of Economics and Statistics]] |volume=90 |issue=3 |pages=414–427 |doi=10.1162/rest.90.3.414  |url=http://www.nber.org/papers/t0344.pdf }}</ref>

== Methods for improving computational efficiency ==
The bootstrap is a powerful technique although may require substantial computing resources in both time and memory. Some techniques have been developed to reduce this burden. They can generally be combined with many of the different types of Bootstrap schemes and various choices of statistics.

=== Parallel processing ===
Most bootstrap methods are [[embarrassingly parallel]] algorithms. That is, the statistic of interest for each bootstrap sample does not depend on other bootstrap samples. Such computations can therefore be performed on separate [[CPU]]s or compute nodes with the results from the separate nodes eventually aggregated for final analysis.

=== Poisson bootstrap ===
The nonparametric bootstrap samples items from a list of size n with counts drawn from a [[multinomial distribution]]. If <math>W_i</math> denotes the number times element i is included in a given bootstrap sample, then each <math>W_i</math> is distributed as a [[binomial distribution]] with n trials and mean 1, but <math>W_i</math> is not independent of <math>W_j</math> for <math>i \neq j</math>.

The Poisson bootstrap instead draws samples assuming all <math>W_i</math>'s are independently and identically distributed as Poisson variables with mean 1.
The rationale is that the limit of the binomial distribution is Poisson:

:<math>\lim_{n\to \infty} \operatorname{Binomial}(n,1/n) = \operatorname{Poisson}(1)</math>

The Poisson bootstrap had been proposed by Hanley and MacGibbon as potentially useful for non-statisticians using software like [[SAS (software)|SAS]] and [[SPSS]], which lacked the bootstrap packages of [[R (programming language)|R]] and [[S-Plus]] programming languages.<ref>{{cite journal
| last1 = Hanley
| first1 = James A.
| last2 = MacGibbon
| first2 = Brenda
| name-list-style = vanc
| title = Creating non-parametric bootstrap samples using Poisson frequencies
| year = 2006
| journal = Computer Methods and Programs in Biomedicine
| volume = 83
| issue = 1
| pages = 57–62
| doi = 10.1016/j.cmpb.2006.04.006
| doi-access = free
| pmid = 16730851
}}</ref> The same authors report that for large enough n, the results are relatively similar to the nonparametric bootstrap estimates but go on to note the Poisson bootstrap has seen minimal use in applications.

Another proposed advantage of the Poisson bootstrap is the independence of the <math>W_i</math> makes the method easier to apply for large datasets that must be processed as streams.<ref>{{cite web |last1= Chamandy|first1=N.|last2= Muralidharan|first2=O.|last3= Najmi|first3=A.|last4= Naidu|first4=S.| name-list-style = vanc | year=2012 |title=Estimating Uncertainty for Massive Data Streams |url=http://www.unofficialgoogledatascience.com/2015/08/an-introduction-to-poisson-bootstrap26.html
|access-date=2024-08-14 }}</ref>

A way to improve on the Poisson bootstrap, termed "sequential bootstrap", is by taking the first samples so that the proportion of unique values is ≈0.632 of the original sample size n. This provides a distribution with main empirical characteristics being within a distance of <math>O(n^{3/4})</math>.<ref>
{{cite journal
| last1 = Babu
| first1 = G. Jogesh
| last2 = Pathak
| first2 = P. K
| last3 = Rao
| first3 = C. R.
| author3-link = C. R. Rao
| title = Second-order correctness of the Poisson bootstrap
| year = 1999
| journal = [[The Annals of Statistics]]
| volume = 27 
| number = 5
| pages = 1666–1683
| doi = 10.1214/aos/1017939146 
| doi-access = free
}}</ref> Empirical investigation has shown this method can yield good results.<ref>{{cite journal
| last1 = Shoemaker
| first1 = Owen J.
| last2 = Pathak
| first2 = P. K.
| title = The sequential bootstrap: a comparison with regular bootstrap
| journal = [[Communications in Statistics - Theory and Methods]]
| volume = 30
| issue = 8–9
| year = 2001
| pages = 1661–1674
| doi = 10.1081/STA-100105691}}</ref> This is related to the reduced bootstrap method.<ref>{{cite journal
| last1 = Jiménez-Gamero
| first1 = María Dolores
| last2 = Muñoz-García 
| first2 = Joaquín
| last3 = Pino-Mejías
| first3 = Rafael
| title = Reduced bootstrap for the median
| journal = [[Statistica Sinica]]
| year = 2004
| volume = 14
| number = 4
| pages = 1179–1198
| jstor = 24307226
}}</ref>

=== Bag of Little Bootstraps ===
For massive data sets, it is often computationally prohibitive to hold all the sample data in memory and resample from the sample data. The Bag of Little Bootstraps (BLB)<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Kleiner|first1=A|last2=Talwalkar|first2=A|last3=Sarkar|first3=P|last4=Jordan|first4=M. I.|title=A scalable bootstrap for massive data|journal=Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series B (Statistical Methodology)|volume=76|issue=4|year=2014|pages=795–816|issn=1369-7412|doi=10.1111/rssb.12050|arxiv=1112.5016|s2cid=3064206}}</ref> provides a method of pre-aggregating data before bootstrapping to reduce computational constraints. This works by partitioning the data set into <math>b</math> equal-sized buckets and aggregating the data within each bucket. This pre-aggregated data set becomes the new sample data over which to draw samples with replacement. This method is similar to the Block Bootstrap, but the motivations and definitions of the blocks are very different. Under certain assumptions, the sample distribution should approximate the full bootstrapped scenario. One constraint is the number of buckets <math>b=n^\gamma </math>where <math>\gamma \in [0.5, 1]</math> and the authors recommend usage of <math>b=n^{0.7}</math> as a general solution.

== Choice of statistic ==

The bootstrap distribution of a point estimator of a population parameter has been used to produce a bootstrapped [[confidence interval]] for the parameter's true value if the parameter can be written as a [[U statistic#statistical functional|function of the population's distribution]].

[[Population parameter]]s are estimated with many [[point estimator]]s. Popular families of point-estimators include [[UMVU|mean-unbiased minimum-variance estimator]]s, [[median-unbiased estimator]]s, [[Bayesian estimator]]s (for example, the [[posterior distribution]]'s [[Bayesian estimator#Posterior mode|mode]], [[Bayesian estimator#Posterior median|median]], [[Bayesian estimator#Posterior mean|mean]]), and [[maximum likelihood|maximum-likelihood estimator]]s.

A Bayesian point estimator and a maximum-likelihood estimator have good performance when the sample size is infinite, according to [[Asymptotic theory (statistics)|asymptotic theory]]. For practical problems with finite samples, other estimators may be preferable. Asymptotic theory suggests techniques that often improve the performance of bootstrapped estimators; the bootstrapping of a maximum-likelihood estimator may often be improved using transformations related to [[pivotal quantity|pivotal quantities]].<ref name="BMA">{{cite book |title=Bootstrap methods and their application |last1=Davison|first1=A. C.|author-link1=Anthony C. Davison|last2=Hinkley|first2=D. V.|author-link2=David V. Hinkley|year=1997 |publisher=Cambridge University Press|series=Cambridge Series in Statistical and Probabilistic Mathematics|isbn= 0-521-57391-2|id=[http://statwww.epfl.ch/davison/BMA/library.html software]}}</ref>

== Deriving confidence intervals from the bootstrap distribution ==
The bootstrap distribution of a parameter-estimator is often used to calculate [[confidence intervals]] for its population-parameter.<ref name="et1993"/> A variety of methods for constructing the confidence intervals have been proposed, although there is disagreement which method is the best.

=== Desirable properties ===
The survey of bootstrap confidence interval methods of DiCiccio and Efron and consequent discussion lists several desired properties of confidence intervals, which generally are not all simultaneously met.

* '''Transformation invariant''' - the confidence intervals from bootstrapping transformed data (e.g., by taking the logarithm) would ideally be the same as transforming the confidence intervals from bootstrapping the untransformed data.
* Confidence intervals should be '''valid''' or '''consistent''', i.e., the probability a parameter is in a confidence interval with nominal level <math>1 - \alpha</math> should be equal to or at least converge in probability to <math>1  - \alpha</math>. The latter criteria is both refined and expanded using the framework of Hall.<ref name="Hall1988"/> The refinements are to distinguish between methods based on how fast the true coverage probability approaches the nominal value, where a method is (using DiCiccio and Efron's terminology) '''first-order accurate''' if the error term in the approximation is <math>O(1 / \sqrt{n})</math> and '''second-order accurate''' if the error term is <math>O(n^{-1})</math>. In addition, methods are distinguished by the speed with which the estimated bootstrap critical point converges to the true (unknown) point, and a method is '''second-order correct''' when this rate is <math>O_p(n^{-3/2})</math>.
* Gleser in the discussion of the paper argues that a limitation of the asymptotic descriptions in the previous bullet is that the <math>O(\cdot)</math> terms are not necessarily uniform in the parameters or true distribution.

=== Bias, asymmetry, and confidence intervals ===
*'''Bias''': The bootstrap distribution and the sample may disagree systematically, in which case  [[Bias (statistics)|bias]] may occur.
*:If the bootstrap distribution of an estimator is symmetric, then percentile confidence-interval are often used; such intervals are appropriate especially for median-unbiased estimators of minimum risk (with respect to an [[absolute value|absolute]] [[loss function]]).  Bias in the bootstrap distribution will lead to bias in the confidence interval.
*:Otherwise, if the bootstrap distribution is non-symmetric, then percentile confidence intervals are often inappropriate.

=== Methods for bootstrap confidence intervals ===
There are several methods for constructing confidence intervals from the bootstrap distribution of a [[real number|real]] parameter:
*'''Basic bootstrap''',<ref name="BMA" /> also known as the '''Reverse Percentile Interval'''.<ref name = hesterberg2014teachers>{{Cite arXiv
  | title = What Teachers Should Know about the Bootstrap: Resampling in the Undergraduate Statistics Curriculum
  | author = Hesterberg, Tim C
  | eprint=1411.5279
  | year = 2014
| class = stat.OT
 }}</ref> The basic bootstrap is a simple scheme to construct the confidence interval: one simply takes the empirical [[quantile]]s from the bootstrap distribution of the parameter (see Davison and Hinkley 1997, equ. 5.6 p.&nbsp;194):
:: <math> (2\widehat{\theta\,} -\theta^{*}_{(1-\alpha/2)},2\widehat{\theta\,} -\theta^{*}_{(\alpha/2)})</math> where <math> \theta^{*}_{(1-\alpha/2)} </math> denotes the <math>1-\alpha/2 </math> [[percentile]] of the bootstrapped coefficients <math> \theta^{*} </math>.

*'''Percentile bootstrap'''. The percentile bootstrap proceeds in a similar way to the basic bootstrap, using percentiles of the bootstrap distribution, but with a different formula (note the inversion of the left and right quantiles):

::<math> (\theta^{*}_{(\alpha/2)},\theta^{*}_{(1-\alpha/2)})</math> where <math> \theta^{*}_{(1-\alpha/2)} </math> denotes the <math>1-\alpha/2 </math> [[percentile]] of the bootstrapped coefficients <math> \theta^{*} </math>.
:See Davison and Hinkley (1997, equ. 5.18 p.&nbsp;203) and Efron and Tibshirani (1993, equ 13.5 p.&nbsp;171).
:This method can be applied to any statistic. It will work well in cases where the bootstrap distribution is symmetrical and centered on the observed statistic<ref>{{Cite book
 | author = Efron, B.
 | author-link = Bradley Efron
 | year = 1982
 | title = The jackknife, the bootstrap, and other resampling plans
 | publisher = Society of Industrial and Applied Mathematics CBMS-NSF Monographs
 | volume = 38
 | isbn = 0-89871-179-7
}}</ref> and where the sample statistic is median-unbiased and has maximum concentration (or minimum risk with respect to an absolute value loss function).  When working with small sample sizes (i.e., less than 50), the basic / reversed percentile and percentile confidence intervals for (for example) the [[variance]] statistic will be too narrow. So that with a sample of 20 points, 90% confidence interval will include the true variance only 78% of the time.<ref name="DAEE">{{cite book|title=Design and Analysis of Ecological Experiments|last1=Scheiner|first1=S.|year=1998|publisher=CRC Press|isbn=0412035618|url-access=registration|url=https://archive.org/details/designanalysisof0000unse}} Ch13, p300</ref>  The basic / reverse percentile confidence intervals are easier to justify mathematically<ref>{{cite book|last1=Rice|first1=John|title=Mathematical Statistics and Data Analysis|page=272|edition=2}} "Although this direct equation of quantiles of the bootstrap sampling distribution with confidence limits may seem initially appealing, it’s rationale is somewhat obscure."</ref><ref name=hesterberg2014teachers /> but they are less accurate in general than percentile confidence intervals, and some authors discourage their use.<ref name=hesterberg2014teachers />
*'''[[Studentization|Studentized]] bootstrap'''. The studentized bootstrap, also called ''bootstrap-t'', is computed analogously to the standard confidence interval, but replaces the quantiles from the normal or student approximation by the quantiles from the bootstrap distribution of the [[Student's t-test]] (see Davison and Hinkley 1997, equ. 5.7 p.&nbsp;194 and Efron and Tibshirani 1993 equ 12.22, p.&nbsp;160):

:: <math> (\widehat{\theta\,} - t^{*}_{(1-\alpha/2)}\cdot \widehat{\text{se}}_\theta,\widehat{\theta\,} - t^{*}_{(\alpha/2)}\cdot \widehat{\text{se}}_\theta) </math> where <math> t^{*}_{(1-\alpha/2)} </math> denotes the <math>1-\alpha/2 </math> [[percentile]] of the bootstrapped [[Student's t-test]] <math> t^{*}=(\widehat{\theta\,}^{*}-\widehat{\theta\,})/\widehat{\text{se}}_{\widehat{\theta\,}^*} </math>, and <math>\widehat{\text{se}}_\theta </math> is the estimated standard error of the coefficient in the original model.

:The studentized test enjoys optimal properties as the statistic that is bootstrapped is [[Pivotal quantity|pivotal]] (i.e. it does not depend on [[nuisance parameter]]s as the t-test follows asymptotically a N(0,1) distribution), unlike the percentile bootstrap.

*'''Bias-corrected bootstrap''' – adjusts for [[Bias (statistics)|bias]] in the bootstrap distribution.
*'''Accelerated bootstrap''' – The bias-corrected and accelerated (BCa) bootstrap, by Efron (1987),<ref name=BCa>{{Cite journal
 | author = Efron, B.
 | author-link = Bradley Efron
 | year = 1987
 | title = Better Bootstrap Confidence Intervals
 | journal = [[Journal of the American Statistical Association]]
 | volume = 82
 | pages = 171–185
 | doi = 10.2307/2289144
 | issue = 397
 | publisher = Journal of the American Statistical Association, Vol. 82, No. 397
 | jstor = 2289144
}}</ref> adjusts for both bias and [[skewness]] in the bootstrap distribution. This approach is accurate in a wide variety of settings, has reasonable computation requirements, and produces reasonably narrow intervals.<ref name="BCa" />

== Bootstrap hypothesis testing ==
{{Cleanup|reason=there are other bootstrap tests|date=July 2023}}
Efron and Tibshirani<ref name="et1993" /> suggest the following algorithm for comparing the means of two independent samples:
Let <math> x_1, \ldots, x_n </math> be a random sample from distribution F with sample mean <math>\bar{x}</math> and sample variance <math>\sigma_x^2</math>. Let <math> y_1, \ldots, y_m </math> be another, independent random sample from distribution G with mean <math>\bar{y}</math> and variance <math>\sigma_y^2</math>

# Calculate the test statistic <math> t = \frac{\bar{x}-\bar{y}}{\sqrt{\sigma_x^2/n + \sigma_y^2/m}} </math>
#Create two new data sets whose values are <math> x_i' = x_i - \bar{x} + \bar{z} </math> and <math> y_i' = y_i - \bar{y} + \bar{z}, </math> where <math>\bar{z}</math> is the mean of the combined sample.
# Draw a random sample (<math> x_i^* </math>) of size <math>n</math> with replacement from <math> x_i' </math> and another random sample (<math> y_i^* </math>) of size <math>m</math> with replacement from <math> y_i' </math>.
# Calculate the test statistic <math> t^* = \frac{\bar{x^*}-\bar{y^*}}{\sqrt{\sigma_x^{*2}/n + \sigma_y^{*2}/m}} </math>
#Repeat 3 and 4 <math>B</math> times (e.g. <math>B=1000</math>) to collect <math>B</math> values of the test statistic.
# Estimate the p-value as <math> p = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^B I\{t_i^* \geq t\}}{B} </math> where <math> I\{\text{condition}\} = 1 </math> when ''condition'' is true and 0 otherwise.

== Example applications ==
{{no footnotes|section|date=June 2012}}

=== Smoothed bootstrap ===
In 1878, [[Simon Newcomb]] took observations on the [[speed of light]].<ref>[http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/book/data/ Data from examples in ''Bayesian Data Analysis'']</ref>
The data set contains two [[outlier]]s, which greatly influence the [[sample mean]]. (The sample mean need not be a [[consistent estimator]] for any [[population mean]], because no mean needs to exist for a [[heavy-tailed distribution]].) A well-defined and  [[robust statistics|robust statistic]] for the central tendency is the sample median, which is consistent and [[median-unbiased estimator|median-unbiased]] for the population median.

The bootstrap distribution for Newcomb's data appears below. We can reduce the discreteness of the bootstrap distribution by adding a small amount of random noise to each bootstrap sample. A conventional choice is to add noise with a standard deviation of <math>\sigma/\sqrt n</math> for a sample size ''n''; this noise is often drawn from a Student-t distribution with ''n-1'' degrees of freedom.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Chihara |first1=Laura |last2=Hesterberg |first2=Tim |title=Mathematical Statistics with Resampling and R |date=3 August 2018 |publisher=John Wiley & Sons, Inc. |doi=10.1002/9781119505969 |isbn=9781119416548 |s2cid=60138121 |edition=2nd |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/book/10.1002/9781119505969}}</ref> This results in an approximately-unbiased estimator for the variance of the sample mean.<ref>Voinov, Vassily [G.]; Nikulin, Mikhail [S.] (1993). Unbiased estimators and their applications. Vol. 1: Univariate case. Dordrect: Kluwer Academic Publishers. ISBN 0-7923-2382-3.</ref>  This means that samples taken from the bootstrap distribution will have a variance which is, on average, equal to the variance of the total population.

Histograms of the bootstrap distribution and the smooth bootstrap distribution appear below. The bootstrap distribution of the sample-median has only a small number of values. The smoothed bootstrap distribution has a richer [[support (measure theory)|support]]. However, note that whether the smoothed or standard bootstrap procedure is favorable is case-by-case and is shown to depend on both the underlying distribution function and on the quantity being estimated.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Young|first=G. A.|date=July 1990|title=Alternative Smoothed Bootstraps|url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1111/j.2517-6161.1990.tb01801.x|journal=Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series B (Methodological)|volume=52|issue=3|pages=477–484|doi=10.1111/j.2517-6161.1990.tb01801.x|issn=0035-9246|url-access=subscription}}</ref>

[[File:MedianHists.png]]

In this example, the bootstrapped 95% (percentile) confidence-interval for the population median is (26, 28.5), which is close to the interval for  (25.98, 28.46) for the smoothed bootstrap.

== Relation to other approaches to inference ==

=== Relationship to other resampling methods ===
{{Further|Resampling (statistics)}}
The bootstrap is distinguished from:
* the [[Jackknife resampling|jackknife]] procedure, used to estimate biases of sample statistics and to estimate variances, and
* [[Cross-validation (statistics)|cross-validation]], in which the parameters (e.g., regression weights, factor loadings) that are estimated in one subsample are applied to another subsample.

[[Bootstrap aggregating]] (bagging) is a [[meta-algorithm]] based on averaging model predictions obtained from models trained on multiple bootstrap samples.

=== U-statistics ===
{{Main|U-statistic}}
In situations where an obvious statistic can be devised to measure a required characteristic using only a small number, ''r'', of data items, a corresponding statistic based on the entire sample can be formulated. Given an ''r''-sample statistic, one can create an ''n''-sample statistic by something similar to bootstrapping (taking the average of the statistic over all subsamples of size ''r''). This procedure is known to have certain good properties and the result is a [[U-statistic]]. The [[sample mean]] and [[sample variance]] are of this form, for ''r''&nbsp;=&nbsp;1 and ''r''&nbsp;=&nbsp;2.

== Asymptotic theory ==
The bootstrap has under certain conditions desirable [[Asymptotic theory (statistics)|asymptotic properties]]. The asymptotic properties most often described are weak convergence / consistency of the [[Stochastic process#Definitions|sample paths]] of the bootstrap empirical process and the validity of [[confidence intervals]] derived from the bootstrap. This section describes the convergence of the empirical bootstrap.

=== Stochastic convergence ===
This paragraph summarizes more complete descriptions of stochastic convergence in van der Vaart and Wellner<ref>{{cite book
| last1 = van der Vaart
| first1 = Aad W.
| author1-link = Aad van der Vaart
| last2 = Wellner
| first2 = Jon A.
| author2-link = Jon A. Wellner
| name-list-style = vanc
| title = Weak Convergence and Empirical Processes With Applications to Statistics
| publisher = [[Springer Science+Business Media]]
| year = 1996
| location = New York
| isbn = 978-1-4757-2547-6
}}</ref> and Kosorok.<ref name="kosorok2008">
{{cite book
| last = Kosorok
| first = Michael R.
| name-list-style = vanc
| title = Introduction to Empirical Processes and Semiparametric Inference
| publisher =  [[Springer Science+Business Media]]
| year = 2008
| location = New York
| isbn = 978-0-387-74977-8
}}</ref> The bootstrap defines a [[stochastic process]], a collection of random variables indexed by some set <math>T</math>, where <math>T</math> is typically the [[real line]] (<math>\mathbb{R}</math>) or a family of functions. Processes of interest are those with bounded sample paths, i.e., sample paths in [[L-infinity]] (<math>\ell^\infty(T)</math>), the set of all [[uniformly bounded]] [[Function (mathematics)|functions]] from <math>T</math> to <math>\mathbb{R}</math>. When equipped with the uniform distance, <math>\ell^\infty(T)</math> is a [[metric space]], and when <math>T = \mathbb{R}</math>, two subspaces of <math>\ell^\infty(T)</math> are of particular interest, <math>C[0,1]</math>, the space of all [[continuous functions]] from <math>T</math> to the [[unit interval]] [0,1], and <math>D[0,1]</math>, the space of all [[cadlag functions]] from <math>T</math> to [0,1]. This is because <math>C[0,1]</math> contains the [[cumulative distribution function|distribution functions]] for all continuous random variables, and <math>D[0,1]</math> contains the distribution functions for all random variables. Statements about the consistency of the bootstrap are statements about the convergence of the sample paths of the bootstrap process as [[random element]]s of the metric space <math>\ell^\infty(T)</math> or some [[Metric space#Definition and illustrations|subspace]] thereof, especially <math>C[0,1]</math> or <math>D[0,1]</math>.

=== Consistency ===
Horowitz in a recent review<ref name="Horowitz2019"/>  defines '''consistency''' as: the bootstrap estimator <math>G_n(\cdot, F_n)</math> is consistent [for a statistic <math>T_n</math>] if, for each <math>F_0</math>, <math>\sup_\tau |G_n(\tau, F_n) - G_\infty(\tau, F_0)|</math> [[Convergence of random variables#Convergence in probability|converges in probability]] to 0 as <math>n \to \infty</math>, where <math>F_n</math> is the empirical distribution of the original sample, <math>F_0</math> is the true but unknown distribution of the statistic, <math>G_\infty(\tau, F_0)</math> is the asymptotic distribution function of <math>T_n</math>, and <math>\tau</math> is the indexing variable in the distribution function, i.e., <math>P(T_n \leq \tau) = G_n(\tau, F_0)</math>. This is sometimes more specifically called '''consistency relative to the Kolmogorov-Smirnov distance'''.<ref>{{cite book
| last = van der Vaart
| first = Aad W.
| author-link = Aad van der Vaart
| name-list-style = vanc
| title = Asymptotic Statistics
| publisher = [[Cambridge University Press]]
| year = 1998
| location = New York
| isbn = 978-0-521-78450-4
| series = Cambridge Series in Statistical and Probabilistic Mathematics
| page = 329
}}</ref>

Horowitz goes on to recommend using a theorem from Mammen<ref>{{cite book
| last = Mammen
| first = Enno
| name-list-style = vanc
| title = When Does Bootstrap Work?: Aysmptotic Results and Simulations
| publisher = [[Springer-Verlag]]
| year = 1992
| location = New York
| isbn = 978-0-387-97867-3
| series = Lecture Notes in Statistics
| volume = 57
}}</ref> 
that provides easier to check necessary and sufficient conditions for consistency for statistics of a certain common form. In particular, let <math>\{X_i : i=1, \ldots, n\}</math> be the random sample. If <math>T_n = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n g_n(X_i) - t_n}{\sigma_n}</math> for a sequence of numbers <math>t_n</math> and <math>\sigma_n</math>, then the bootstrap estimate of the cumulative distribution function estimates the empirical cumulative distribution function if and only if <math>T_n</math> [[Convergence of random variables#Convergence in distribution|converges in distribution]] to the [[standard normal distribution]].

=== Strong consistency ===
Convergence in (outer) probability as described above is also called '''weak consistency'''. It can also be shown with slightly stronger assumptions, that the bootstrap is '''strongly consistent''', where convergence in (outer) probability is replaced by convergence (outer) almost surely. When only one type of consistency is described, it is typically weak consistency. This is adequate for most statistical applications since it implies confidence bands derived from the bootstrap are asymptotically valid.<ref name="kosorok2008"/>

=== Showing consistency using the central limit theorem ===
In simpler cases, it is possible to use the [[central limit theorem]] directly to show the [[consistency (statistics)|consistency]] of the bootstrap procedure for estimating the distribution of the sample mean.

Specifically, let us consider <math> X_{n1}, \ldots, X_{nn} </math> independent identically distributed random variables with <math> \mathbb{E}[X_{n1}] = \mu </math> and <math> \text{Var}[X_{n1}] = \sigma^2 < \infty </math> for each <math> n \ge 1 </math>. Let <math> \bar{X}_n = n^{-1}(X_{n1} + \cdots + X_{nn}) </math>. In addition, for each <math> n \ge 1 </math>, conditional on <math> X_{n1}, \ldots, X_{nn} </math>, let <math>X^*_{n1}, \ldots, X^*_{nn}</math> be independent random variables with distribution equal to the empirical distribution of <math> X_{n1}, \ldots, X_{nn} </math>. This is the sequence of bootstrap samples.

Then it can be shown that
<math display='block'> \sup_{\tau \in \mathbb{R}} \left | P^* \left(\frac{\sqrt{n} (\bar{X}^*_n - \bar{X}_n)}{\hat{\sigma}_n} \le \tau \right) - P \left(\frac{\sqrt{n} (\bar{X}_n - \mu)}{\sigma} \le \tau \right) \right | \to 0 \text{ in probability as } n \to \infty, </math>
where <math> P^* </math> represents probability conditional on <math> X_{n1}, \ldots, X_{nn} </math>, <math> n \ge 1 </math>, <math> \bar{X}^*_n = n^{-1}(X^*_{n1} + \cdots + X^*_{nn}) </math>, and <math> \hat{\sigma}_n^2 = n^{-1} \sum_{i=1}^{n}(X_{ni} - \bar{X}_n)^2 </math>.

To see this, note that <math>(X_{ni}^* - \bar X_n)/\sqrt n\hat{\sigma}_n</math> satisfies the [[Lindeberg condition]], so the CLT holds.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Gregory |first=Karl |date=29 Dec 2023 |title=Some results based on the Lindeberg central limit theorem |url=https://people.stat.sc.edu/gregorkb/STAT_824_sp_2023/STAT_824_Lec_11_supplement.pdf |access-date=29 Dec 2023}}</ref>

The [[Glivenko–Cantelli theorem]] provides theoretical background for the bootstrap method.

== Finite populations ==
[[Finite population]]s and [[urn problem|drawing without replacement]] require adaptations of the bootstrap due to the violation of the i.i.d assumption. One example is "population bootstrap"<ref>Mashreghi, Zeinab, David Haziza, and Christian Léger. "A survey of bootstrap methods in finite population sampling." (2016): 1-52. https://projecteuclid.org/journals/statistics-surveys/volume-10/issue-none/A-survey-of-bootstrap-methods-in-finite-population-sampling/10.1214/16-SS113.full</ref>.
